items.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025
items.q: I played with Al Cohn and Zoot Sims, with Stan Getz for a little while. You know I was playing a lot of gigs. And Bobby Hackett. You know gigs in New York mostly, sometimes on the road like Chicago or someplace. I think I went to Detroit with Stan, Chicago.

ctx.x: Oh that’s a great one. I had a question down the road, advice to students, and you just nailed it. Do you ever tell them be aware of what bass player you’re joining?

Absolutely. Bass players have been my — the people that have pushed me forward the most and the first that I can really remember was Red Mitchell who befriended me when I was about 17, but I already knew some other people, and I was a Jazzbo man. I went to see everybody play. And I got to meet everybody and I was hanging out at the drum shop every day. So I was on the scene and I wanted to be a part of the scene, and I was part of the scene. I just wasn’t really a good drummer but like I say I could play. But it…

Levy, the great bebop drummer who befriended me and kind of essentially threatened me to become a better drummer, told me that I wasn’t — that I had a lot of possibilities but I wasn’t making it technically and I had to practice and get my hands together. And the way he said it, I don’t know if you know this about Stan but he was an ex-boxer from Philadelphia. Big guy, very brutal looking guy. He was a sweet man, a wonderful guy, but he looked at you in a way, it was like I’m going to kill you if you don’t do…
